statement: In adults with a hangover, whether drinking water prevents or relieves it had not been tested in any experimental study up to July 2024, as described in a narrative review (Mackus et al., 2024). In the review authors' own re-analysis of 176 people with a hangover on a long walk, those who drank more water had worse hangovers, but the amount drunk was not related to how much their hangover or their thirst changed during the day; in student surveys, water was the most used remedy and was rated about 5 to 6 out of 10 for how well it worked. After a night of heavy drinking, thirst was clearly raised only in the morning, while the hangover lasted all day, and small old studies found mild, short-lived changes in fluid balance, which the authors read as dehydration and hangover being separate effects of drinking. Evidence is insufficient to say whether water helps; the figures are second-hand or the authors' own re-analysis. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Nobody had tested whether drinking water stops or cures a hangover; thirst faded by late morning, but the hangover stayed.
population: Adults with a hangover: 176 walkers in Crete (authors' re-analysis), Dutch students (surveys) and small groups of men in old laboratory studies
exposure: Drinking water during a hangover day (amount self-reported) or as a remedy during or after drinking (survey ratings)
comparator: People who drank less water on the same walk (correlation); no untreated comparison in the surveys
outcome: Hangover severity and thirst ratings and their change during the day; perceived efficacy of water; markers of dehydration
magnitude: Water drunk against hangover severity before, during and after the walk: r = 0.176, 0.243 and 0.229 (p from 0.019 to below 0.001); against change in hangover severity r = 0.103 (p = 0.174), 0.017 (p = 0.828) and 0.066 (p = 0.388); against thirst and change in thirst |r| no more than 0.061, none significant. Survey efficacy ratings for water 5.2 to 5.8 out of 10. Thirst above an alcohol-free day only at the 09:30 and 10:30 ratings; hangover above it at every rating to 15:30.

evidence.locator: Limitations and future research, single paragraph running from p. 15; p. 16, left column, sentence beginning 'Finally'
evidence.extracted: The authors state that no experimental study had specifically investigated whether drinking water could counteract dehydration or the alcohol hangover.

evidence.locator: The impact of drinking water on hangover severity, 3rd study (p. 14, right column) and continuation (p. 15, 1st paragraph)
evidence.extracted: Re-analysis restricted to the 176 of 307 walkers with a hangover: water drunk during the walk correlated with hangover severity before (r = 0.176, p = 0.019), during (r = 0.243, p < 0.001) and after (r = 0.229, p = 0.002), but not significantly with change in hangover severity (r = 0.103, p = 0.174; r = 0.017, p = 0.828; r = 0.066, p = 0.388).
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mackus_2024_HangoverDehydrationWater.pdf (published version, Alcohol 2024;121:9-18), read in full

evidence.extracted: Water drunk was not significantly correlated with thirst before, during or after the walk (r = -0.028, p = 0.714; r = -0.001, p = 0.993; r = 0.059, p = 0.435) or with changes in thirst (r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046).
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mackus_2024_HangoverDehydrationWater.pdf (published version, Alcohol 2024;121:9-18), read in full

evidence.locator: Left column, paragraph beginning 'Experimental data from a naturalistic study', continued at the top of the right column; Fig. 5
evidence.extracted: After an evening of heavy drinking (amount on the study card), hangover severity was significantly higher than on an alcohol-free day at every hourly rating from 09:30 to 15:30, while thirst was significantly higher only at 09:30 and 10:30.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mackus_2024_HangoverDehydrationWater.pdf (published version, Alcohol 2024;121:9-18), read in full

evidence.locator: The impact of drinking water on hangover severity, 1st and 2nd studies
evidence.extracted: In a survey of 462 Dutch students water was the most used hangover remedy (55.8%) and was rated 5.8 out of 10 for efficacy while hungover; in a survey of 826 students, water during drinking was rated 5.2 (SD 2.4, N = 618) and water before bed 5.6 (SD 2.6, N = 502); the amount of water was not recorded.

evidence.locator: Limitations and future research, 1st paragraph (right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors note that the 13 publications comprised 10 experimental studies, several more than 40 years old with small samples, and 3 surveys relying on retrospective self-report, and that studies usually did not sufficiently control for food, physical activity or sleep in their analyses.

risk_of_bias.note: Correlations in which people who felt worse drank more water (confounding by indication), a post hoc re-analysis by the authors of their own data, and remedy ratings without a comparison; source is a narrative review.

indirectness.note: A long walk in the heat, old laboratory studies in a few men, and ratings of perceived efficacy rather than measured effects of water.

imprecision.note: Not applicable: no estimate of the effect of water exists.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence summarized in a narrative review starts low; downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). It complements the later small trial of water during drinking, which found no detectable effect (Imai et al., 2026, a separate claim). The authors' conclusion that water is not effective is not adopted: no trial existed, so the finding is that the question is untested.
